subject: maths
title: Place Value, Rounding and Negative Numbers up to 10,000,000
seo_title: Year 6 Place Value and Rounding Worksheets: Numbers to 10 Million and Negative Numbers (Free)
standard_text: Read, write, order and compare numbers up to 10,000,000 and determine the value of each digit; round any whole number to a required degree of accuracy; use negative numbers in context, and calculate intervals across zero; solve number and practical problems that involve all of the above.
meta_desc: Free Year 6 maths worksheets for the National Curriculum: place value up to 10,000,000, numbers in words, comparing and ordering, rounding to any place, and negative numbers with intervals across zero. 100 SATs-style questions with an answer key.
key_big: Split big numbers into groups of three: millions, thousands, ones. The place decides what each digit is worth.
key_sub: Write 0 in every empty place (4,060,005). To round, look one place to the right: 5 or more rounds up. Across zero, jump to 0 and add: −7 to 5 is 7 + 5 = 12.
body_html:
Place value up to 10,000,000

Big numbers are split into groups of three digits: millions, thousands and ones. Each group has hundreds, tens and ones. Each place is worth 10 times the place to its right.

Reading and writing large numbers

Read each group of three digits, then say its name: million, thousand. In words we write “and” before the last tens and ones.

DigitsWords
4,060,005four million, sixty thousand and five
3,250,412three million, two hundred and fifty thousand, four hundred and twelve
10,000,000ten million
Words to digits

Write two million, three hundred and five thousand and forty in digits.

2 million → 2. Three hundred and five thousand → 305. Forty → 040 (no hundreds, so write 0).

Answer: 2,305,040

Compare and order

First count the digits: a 7-digit number is greater than any 6-digit number. If both have the same number of digits, compare place by place from the left until two digits are different.

Compare

5,710,200 ☐ 5,701,200

Millions: 5 = 5. Hundred thousands: 7 = 7. Ten thousands: 1 > 0.

Answer: 5,710,200 > 5,701,200

Rounding to any place

  1. Find the digit in the place you are rounding to.
  2. Look at the digit one place to its right.
  3. 5 or more: round up. 4 or less: round down.
  4. Change every digit after the rounding place to 0.
Round 3,462,718 to the nearestLook atAnswer
10the ones digit: 83,462,720
100the tens digit: 13,462,700
1,000the hundreds digit: 73,463,000
10,000the thousands digit: 23,460,000
100,000the ten thousands digit: 63,500,000
1,000,000the hundred thousands digit: 43,000,000
Watch the 9s

Round 4,965,300 to the nearest 100,000.

The hundred thousands digit is 9 and the ten thousands digit is 6, so round up. 9 + 1 = 10 hundred thousands. Exchange them for 1 million: 4,900,000 + 100,000 = 5,000,000.

Answer: 5,000,000

Negative numbers and intervals across zero

Numbers below 0 are negative. We meet them in temperatures, below sea level and in lifts. To find the difference between a negative and a positive number, jump to 0 first, then add the two jumps.

Temperature

The temperature rose from −7 °C to 5 °C. By how many degrees did it rise?

7 degrees up to 0 °C, then 5 more degrees: 7 + 5 = 12.

Answer: 12 degrees

Calculate

−6 − 5

Start at −6 and count down 5. Going down from a negative number makes it more negative.

Answer: −11

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Missing a zero placeholder (four million, sixty thousand and five → 4,600,005)Write each group as three digits: 4 | 060 | 005 → 4,060,005
Giving the digit, not its value (the 6 in 4,060,005 is 6)It is in the ten thousands place: 60,000
Rounding the wrong place (3,462,718 to the nearest 100,000 → 3,463,000)Find the hundred thousands digit first: 3,500,000
Keeping the digits after rounding (3,462,718 to the nearest 100,000 → 3,562,718)Change every digit after the place to 0
Interval across zero as 7 − 5 = 2 (−7 °C to 5 °C)Jump to 0 and add: 7 + 5 = 12

faq.q: What place value do Year 6 children need to know?
faq.a: Year 6 pupils read, write, order and compare numbers up to 10,000,000 and know the value of every digit. They round any whole number to a required degree of accuracy and use negative numbers in context, including finding intervals across zero.

faq.q: How do you write a number in the millions in words?
faq.a: Split it into groups of three digits and read each group with its name. 4,060,005 is “four million, sixty thousand and five”. Write 0 in every empty place when you turn words back into digits.

faq.q: How do you find the difference between a negative and a positive number?
faq.a: Count to 0 and then on from 0, and add the two parts. From −7 °C to 5 °C is 7 + 5 = 12 degrees, not 7 − 5.

faq.q: Is place value tested in the Year 6 SATs?
faq.a: Yes. The KS2 reasoning papers often ask pupils to round, order large numbers or find a difference across zero. A scaled score of 100 or more means a pupil has met the expected standard.

sets.title: Value of each digit up to 10,000,000 and numbers in words

items.q: What is the value of the red digit?
items.e: The red 5 is in the hundred thousands place, so it is worth 5 hundred thousands = 500,000. The digit is 5, but its value is 500,000.

items.q: What is the value of the red digit?
items.e: The red 1 is in the thousands place, so it is worth 1 thousand = 1,000. The digit is 1, but its value is 1,000.

items.q: What is the value of the red digit?
items.e: The red 4 is in the millions place, so it is worth 4 million = 4,000,000. The digit is 4, but its value is 4,000,000.

items.q: In 3,278,965, which digit is in the hundred thousands place?
items.e: Read the places from the right: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, hundred thousands, millions. In 3,278,965 the hundred thousands digit is 2, worth 200,000.

items.q: In 1,873,049, which digit is in the ten thousands place?
items.e: Read the places from the right: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, hundred thousands, millions. In 1,873,049 the ten thousands digit is 7, worth 70,000.

items.q: What is the value of the red digit?
items.e: The red 7 is in the ten thousands place, so it is worth 7 ten thousands = 70,000. The digit is 7, but its value is 70,000.

items.q: What is the value of the red digit?
items.e: The red 1 is in the hundreds place, so it is worth 1 hundred = 100. The digit is 1, but its value is 100.

items.q: What is the value of the digit 1 in 2,316,049?
items.e: The 1 is in the ten thousands place, so it is worth 1 ten thousand = 10,000. The digit is 1, but its value is 10,000.

items.q: What is the value of the digit 9 in 7,956,023?
items.e: The 9 is in the hundred thousands place, so it is worth 9 hundred thousands = 900,000. The digit is 9, but its value is 900,000.

items.q: What is the value of the digit 4 in 2,194,367?
items.e: The 4 is in the thousands place, so it is worth 4 thousands = 4,000. The digit is 4, but its value is 4,000.

items.q: What is the value of the digit 1 in 1,287,609?
items.e: The 1 is in the millions place, so it is worth 1 million = 1,000,000. The digit is 1, but its value is 1,000,000.

items.q: Which number has a 5 in the hundred thousands place?
items.e: The hundred thousands place is the 6th digit from the right (the first digit after the millions). In 8,562,937 the 5 is there, so it is worth 500,000.
Put each digit in its place and write 0 in every empty place: 3,000,000 + 400,000 + 7,000 + 20 = 3,407,020.
Put each digit in its place and write 0 in every empty place: 6,000,000 + 50,000 + 300 = 6,050,300.

items.q: Which number is four million, sixty thousand and five?
items.e: Write each part in its group of three digits: four million → 4, sixty thousand → 060, then 005. Fill every empty place with 0: 4,060,005.

items.q: Which number is two million, three hundred and seven thousand and eighty?
items.e: Write each part in its group of three digits: two million → 2, three hundred and seven thousand → 307, then 080. Fill every empty place with 0: 2,307,080.

items.q: Which number is nine million, four thousand, three hundred?
items.e: Write each part in its group of three digits: nine million → 9, four thousand → 004, then 300. Fill every empty place with 0: 9,004,300.

items.q: How do you write 5,030,700 in words?
c: five million, three thousand, seven hundred
five million, thirty thousand, seven hundred
five million, three hundred thousand, seven hundred
items.e: Split 5,030,700 into groups: 5 million, 30 thousand, 700. Say each group, then its name: five million, thirty thousand, seven hundred.

items.q: How do you write 1,406,020 in words?
c: one million, four hundred and sixty thousand and twenty
one million, four hundred thousand, six hundred and twenty
one million, four hundred and six thousand and twenty
one million, forty-six thousand and twenty
items.e: Split 1,406,020 into groups: 1 million, 406 thousand, 20. Say each group, then its name: one million, four hundred and six thousand and twenty.

items.q: In 3,606,000, how many times greater is the value of the first 6 than the value of the second 6?
items.e: The first 6 is worth 600,000. The second 6 is worth 6,000. 600,000 ÷ 6,000 = 100. Each place to the left is worth 10 times more, and the 6s are two places apart: 10 × 10 = 100. (594,000 is the difference, not how many times greater.)

sets.title: Compare and order numbers up to 10,000,000

items.q: Which is true?
items.e: Compare from the left. The digits are the same until the ten thousands place: 9 ten thousands is more than 8 ten thousands. So 6,098,450 > 6,089,450.

items.q: Which is true?
items.e: 1,002,300 has 7 digits and 987,654 has only 6, so 1,002,300 is greater. Big first digits do not matter when a number has fewer digits.

items.q: Which is true?
items.e: Compare from the left. The digits are the same until the ten thousands place: 1 ten thousand is more than 0 ten thousands. So 5,710,200 > 5,701,200.

items.q: Which is true?
items.e: Compare from the left. The digits are the same until the hundred thousands place: 4 hundred thousands is more than 0 hundred thousands. So 3,405,600 > 3,045,600.

items.q: What is 10,000 more than 4,995,300?
items.e: Add 1 to the ten thousands digit: 9 ten thousands + 1 = 10 ten thousands. Exchange them for 1 hundred thousand, then 9 + 1 = 10 hundred thousands, so exchange again for 1 million. 4,995,300 + 10,000 = 5,005,300.

items.q: What is 100,000 less than 2,034,500?
items.e: There are 0 hundred thousands, so exchange 1 million for 10 hundred thousands. 10 − 1 = 9 hundred thousands and 1 million is left. 2,034,500 − 100,000 = 1,934,500.

items.q: Which number is the greatest?
items.e: Compare from the left. The digits are the same until the hundred thousands place: 5 hundred thousands is more than 3 hundred thousands. So 4,523,976 > 4,395,276. 4,523,976 is the greatest.

items.q: Which number is the greatest?
items.e: Compare from the left. The digits are the same until the ten thousands place: 5 ten thousands is more than 1 ten thousand. So 3,651,284 > 3,612,584. 3,651,284 is the greatest.

items.q: Which number is the greatest?
items.e: 998,750 has only 6 digits, so it is the smallest, even though it starts with 9. Of the 7-digit numbers: Compare from the left. The digits are the same until the ten thousands place: 9 ten thousands is more than 8 ten thousands. So 1,098,000 > 1,089,000. 1,098,000 is the greatest.

items.q: Which number is the smallest?
items.e: Compare from the left. The digits are the same until the thousands place: 7 thousands is more than 6 thousands. So 2,817,496 > 2,816,794. 2,816,794 is the smallest.

items.q: Which number is the smallest?
items.e: Compare from the left. The digits are the same until the hundred thousands place: 9 hundred thousands is more than 3 hundred thousands. So 8,937,451 > 8,379,451. 8,379,451 is the smallest.

items.q: Which number is the smallest?
items.e: 999,999 has only 6 digits, so it is the smallest. Every 7-digit number is at least 1,000,000.

items.q: What number does the arrow point to?
items.e: From 2,000,000 to 3,000,000 there are 10 equal jumps, so each mark is 100,000, not 10,000. The arrow is 7 marks after 2,000,000: 2,000,000 + 700,000 = 2,700,000.

items.q: What number does the arrow point to?
items.e: From 5,000,000 to 6,000,000 there are 10 equal jumps, so each mark is 100,000, not 10,000. The arrow is 4 marks after 5,000,000: 5,000,000 + 400,000 = 5,400,000.

items.q: Put 3,692,857, 3,692,785, 3,695,287 in order from smallest to greatest.
Put 1,528,476, 1,528,647, 1,524,786 in order from smallest to greatest.
Put 7,892,346, 7,893,426, 7,829,436 in order from greatest to smallest.
items.e: Compare from the left. 7,829,436 < 7,892,346 (ten thousands: 2 < 9). 7,892,346 < 7,893,426 (thousands: 2 < 3). So the order is 7,893,426, 7,892,346, 7,829,436.

items.q: 5,2☐8,400 > 5,276,000. Which digit could go in the box?
items.e: The millions and hundred thousands are the same. Compare the ten thousands: the box must be more than 7, or equal to 7. 4, 5 and 6 are too small. 5,288,400 > 5,276,000.

items.q: 3,☐45,000 < 3,412,900. Which digit could go in the box?
items.e: The millions are the same. Compare the hundred thousands: the box must be less than 4. If it is 4, compare the ten thousands: 4 > 1, so 3,445,000 would be too big. 3,345,000 < 3,412,900.

items.q: Use each of the digits 4, 0, 8, 2, 6, 1 and 9 once. What is the greatest 7-digit number you can make?
items.e: Put the biggest digit in the millions place, then the next biggest, and so on: 9, 8, 6, 4, 2, 1, 0. The greatest number is 9,864,210.

items.q: Round 910,721 to the nearest 1,000.
items.e: 910,721 is between 910,000 and 911,000. Look at the hundreds digit: 7. 5 or more, so round up. Answer: 911,000.

items.q: Round 445,881 to the nearest 10,000.
items.e: 445,881 is between 440,000 and 450,000. Look at the thousands digit: 5. 5 or more, so round up. Answer: 450,000.

items.q: Round 8,867,707 to the nearest 10.
items.e: 8,867,707 is between 8,867,700 and 8,867,710. Look at the ones digit: 7. 5 or more, so round up. Answer: 8,867,710.

items.q: Round 134,246 to the nearest 100.
items.e: 134,246 is between 134,200 and 134,300. Look at the tens digit: 4. 4 or less, so round down. Answer: 134,200.

items.q: Round 4,210,267 to the nearest 100,000.
items.e: 4,210,267 is between 4,200,000 and 4,300,000. Look at the ten thousands digit: 1. 4 or less, so round down. Answer: 4,200,000.

items.q: Round 2,645,214 to the nearest 1,000,000.
items.e: 2,645,214 is between 2,000,000 and 3,000,000. Look at the hundred thousands digit: 6. 5 or more, so round up. Answer: 3,000,000.

items.q: Round 8,106,033 to the nearest 1,000.
items.e: 8,106,033 is between 8,106,000 and 8,107,000. Look at the hundreds digit: 0. 4 or less, so round down. Answer: 8,106,000.

items.q: Round 3,387,993 to the nearest 10,000.
items.e: 3,387,993 is between 3,380,000 and 3,390,000. Look at the thousands digit: 7. 5 or more, so round up. Answer: 3,390,000.

items.q: Round 2,450,000 to the nearest 100,000.
items.e: 2,450,000 is exactly halfway between 2,400,000 and 2,500,000. A number that is exactly halfway rounds up. Answer: 2,500,000.

items.q: Round 3,500,000 to the nearest 1,000,000.
items.e: 3,500,000 is exactly halfway between 3,000,000 and 4,000,000. A number that is exactly halfway rounds up. Answer: 4,000,000.

items.q: Round 1,140,478 to the nearest 10,000.
items.e: 1,140,478 is between 1,140,000 and 1,150,000. Look at the thousands digit: 0. 4 or less, so round down. Answer: 1,140,000.

items.q: Round 757,468 to the nearest 100,000.
items.e: 757,468 is between 700,000 and 800,000. Look at the ten thousands digit: 5. 5 or more, so round up. Answer: 800,000.

items.q: Round 3,828,038 to the nearest 100,000.
items.e: 3,828,038 is between 3,800,000 and 3,900,000. Look at the ten thousands digit: 2. 4 or less, so round down. Answer: 3,800,000.

items.q: Round 7,025,759 to the nearest 1,000,000.
items.e: 7,025,759 is between 7,000,000 and 8,000,000. Look at the hundred thousands digit: 0. 4 or less, so round down. Answer: 7,000,000.

items.q: Round 4,965,300 to the nearest 100,000.
items.e: 4,965,300 is between 4,900,000 and 5,000,000. Look at the ten thousands digit: 6. 5 or more, so round up. The hundred thousands digit is 9, so rounding up makes 10 hundred thousands. Exchange them for 1 million. Answer: 5,000,000.

items.q: Round 2,397,800 to the nearest 10,000.
items.e: 2,397,800 is between 2,390,000 and 2,400,000. Look at the thousands digit: 7. 5 or more, so round up. The ten thousands digit is 9, so rounding up makes 10 ten thousands. Exchange them for 1 hundred thousand. Answer: 2,400,000.

items.q: Which number rounds to 4,000,000 when you round to the nearest 1,000,000?
items.e: Numbers from 3,500,000 to 4,499,999 round to 4,000,000. 3,612,000 is in that range. 3,450,000 rounds to 3,000,000.

items.q: Which number rounds to 760,000 when you round to the nearest 10,000?
items.e: Numbers from 755,000 to 764,999 round to 760,000. 756,300 is in that range. 765,000 rounds to 770,000.

items.q: What is the smallest whole number that rounds to 300,000 when you round to the nearest 100,000?
items.e: Numbers from 250,000 to 349,999 round to 300,000. 249,999 has 4 ten thousands, so it rounds down to 200,000. The smallest is 250,000.

items.q: Round 6,348,527 to the nearest 1,000, the nearest 100,000 and the nearest 1,000,000. Which list is correct?
items.e: Always round the number you started with. Nearest 1,000: the hundreds digit is 5, so 6,349,000. Nearest 100,000: the ten thousands digit is 4, so 6,300,000. Nearest 1,000,000: the hundred thousands digit is 3, so 6,000,000.

sets.title: Negative numbers and intervals across zero

items.q: What number does the arrow point to?
items.e: The arrow is to the left of 0, so the number is negative. Start at −5 and count 2 marks to the left: −7. Numbers get smaller as you go left.

items.q: What number does the arrow point to?
items.e: The arrow is to the left of 0, so the number is negative. Start at −10 and count 3 marks to the left: −13. Numbers get smaller as you go left.

items.q: What number does the arrow point to?
items.e: The arrow is to the left of 0, so the number is negative. Start at −15 and count 1 mark to the left: −16. Numbers get smaller as you go left.

items.q: What temperature does the thermometer show?
items.e: The red line ends below 0, so the temperature is negative. Each mark is 1 degree. Start at −5 °C and count down 4 marks to the top of the red line: −9 °C.

items.q: What temperature does the thermometer show?
items.e: The red line ends below 0, so the temperature is negative. Each mark is 1 degree. Start at 0 °C and count down 4 marks to the top of the red line: −4 °C.

items.q: The numbers go down by 7 each time: 19, 12, 5, ? What comes next?
items.e: The numbers go down by 7 each time. 5 − 7: count down 5 to 0, then 2 more: −2.

items.q: Put these temperatures in order from coldest to warmest: −3 °C, −8 °C, 2 °C, −1 °C.
items.e: Below 0, the bigger the number after the minus sign, the colder it is. −8 °C is the coldest and 2 °C is the only one above 0. Order: −8 °C, −3 °C, −1 °C, 2 °C.

items.q: Which temperature is the warmest?
items.e: All four are below 0. The warmest is the closest to 0: −2 °C is only 2 degrees below 0.

items.q: The dots show −7 and 5. What is the difference between them?
items.e: Count in two jumps through 0. From −7 to 0 is 7. From 0 to 5 is 5. 7 + 5 = 12. Do not work out 7 − 5.

items.q: The dots show −4 and 8. What is the difference between them?
items.e: Count in two jumps through 0. From −4 to 0 is 4. From 0 to 8 is 8. 4 + 8 = 12. Do not work out 8 − 4.

items.q: Calculate −4 + 9.
items.e: Start at −4 and count up 9: 5. You pass 0 on the way.

items.q: Calculate 3 − 8.
items.e: Start at 3 and count down 8. Count down to 0 (3), then 5 more below 0: −5.

items.q: The numbers go down by 6 each time: 15, 9, 3, ? What comes next?
items.e: The numbers go down by 6 each time. 3 − 6: count down 3 to 0, then 3 more: −3.

items.q: What number is exactly halfway between −6 and 10?
items.e: The difference between −6 and 10 is 6 + 10 = 16. Half of 16 is 8. Count 8 up from −6: −6 + 8 = 2. (8 is the size of the half, not the number.)

items.q: What is the difference between −12 and 6?
items.e: Count in two jumps through 0. From −12 to 0 is 12. From 0 to 6 is 6. 12 + 6 = 18. Do not work out 12 − 6.

items.q: What is the difference between −15 and −6?
items.e: Both numbers are below 0. Count up from −15 to −6: 15 − 6 = 9.

items.q: What is the difference between 9 and −13?
items.e: Count in two jumps through 0. From −13 to 0 is 13. From 0 to 9 is 9. 13 + 9 = 22. Do not work out 13 − 9.

items.q: Calculate −6 − 5.
items.e: Start at −6 and count down 5. Going down from a negative number makes it more negative: −11.

items.q: Calculate −12 + 7.
items.e: Start at −12 and count up 7. You stay below 0: −5.

items.q: −3 − ☐ = −10. What number goes in the box?
items.e: From −3 down to −10 is 7 steps, so take away 7. Check: −3 − 7 = −10.

sets.title: Place value, rounding and negative number word problems

items.q: At the 2021 census, Birmingham had a population of 1,144,919. What is the value of the first 4 in this number?
items.e: 1,144,919 has 1 million, 1 hundred thousand, 4 ten thousands, 4 thousands, 9 hundreds, 1 ten and 9 ones. The first 4 is in the ten thousands place, so it is worth 40,000.

items.q: A house was sold for £348,750. What is the price to the nearest £10,000?
items.e: 348,750 is between 340,000 and 350,000. Look at the thousands digit: 8. 5 or more, so round up. Answer: £350,000.

items.q: One winter day in Edinburgh the temperature was −6 °C at 6 am and 7 °C at 2 pm. By how many degrees did the temperature rise?
items.e: Count in two jumps through 0. From −6 °C to 0 °C is 6. From 0 °C to 7 °C is 7. 6 + 7 = 13 degrees. Do not work out 7 − 6.

items.q: These are the populations of four cities at the 2021 census: Sheffield 556,521; Bristol 472,465; Leeds 811,953; Manchester 551,938. Which list orders the cities from greatest to smallest population?
items.e: Leeds is the only one with 8 hundred thousands, and Bristol has only 4. Sheffield and Manchester both have 5 hundred thousands and 5 ten thousands; compare the thousands: 6 > 1. Order: Leeds, Sheffield, Manchester, Bristol.

items.q: A diver is 12 m below sea level. A seagull is flying 15 m above sea level, straight above the diver. How far apart are they?
items.e: From 12 m below sea level up to sea level is 12 m. From sea level up to the seagull is 15 m. 12 + 15 = 27 m. (15 − 12 = 3 is the mistake of not crossing 0.)

items.q: The average distance from the Earth to the Moon is 384,400 km. What is this to the nearest 10,000 km?
items.e: 384,400 is between 380,000 and 390,000. Look at the thousands digit: 4. 4 or less, so round down. Answer: 380,000 km.

items.q: A football club’s total attendance for the season was two million, forty thousand and fifty. How is this written in digits?
items.e: 2 million → 2, forty thousand → 040, fifty → 050. Fill every empty place with 0: 2,040,050.

items.q: At the 2021 census, Leeds had a population of 811,953. What is this rounded to the nearest 10,000?
items.e: 811,953 is between 810,000 and 820,000. Look at the thousands digit: 1. 4 or less, so round down. Answer: 810,000 people.

items.q: A crowd of 74,310 fans watched a cup final. What is the crowd to the nearest 1,000?
items.e: 74,310 is between 74,000 and 75,000. Look at the hundreds digit: 3. 4 or less, so round down. Answer: 74,000 fans.

items.q: In a shopping centre, the ground floor is level 0 and the car park levels are −1 and −2. George takes the lift from level 3 down to level −2. How many levels does he go down?
items.e: From level 3 down to 0 is 3 levels. From 0 down to −2 is 2 levels. 3 + 2 = 5 levels.

items.q: At 6 pm the temperature was 3 °C. During the night it fell by 9 degrees. What was the temperature then?
items.e: Fell means count down. Count down 3 to reach 0, then 6 more: −6 °C. (3 − 9 is not 6.)

items.q: A museum had 1,463,000 visitors in a year. Arjun rounds this to the nearest 100,000 first, then rounds his answer to the nearest 1,000,000 and gets 2,000,000. What is 1,463,000 rounded to the nearest 1,000,000?
items.e: Always round the original number. Look at the hundred thousands digit of 1,463,000: 4. 4 or less, so round down to 1,000,000. Rounding twice (1,463,000 → 1,500,000 → 2,000,000) gives the wrong answer.

items.q: A newspaper says “about 60,000 fans” went to a concert. The number was rounded to the nearest 1,000. Which could be the real number of fans?
items.e: Numbers from 59,500 to 60,499 round to 60,000. 59,612 is in that range. 60,512 and 60,500 round up to 61,000, and 59,412 rounds down to 59,000.

items.q: A submarine is at −250 m (250 m below sea level). It rises 180 m. Where is it now?
items.e: Rising means count up. −250 + 180: it is still 70 m below sea level, so −70 m.

items.q: A theme park had 1,995,800 visitors last year. This year it had 10,000 more. How many visitors did it have this year?
items.e: Add 1 to the ten thousands digit: 9 + 1 = 10, so exchange for 1 hundred thousand. Then 9 + 1 = 10 hundred thousands, so exchange for 1 million. 1,995,800 + 10,000 = 2,005,800.

items.q: At midnight the temperature was −8 °C. By 9 am it had risen by 5 degrees. What was the temperature at 9 am?
items.e: Risen means count up. From −8 °C count up 5: −7, −6, −5, −4, −3. It is still below 0: −3 °C.

items.q: Isla has the digit cards 7, 0, 3, 9, 1, 5 and 2. She uses each card once to make the smallest 7-digit number she can. What number does she make?
items.e: Put the smallest digits first, but a 7-digit number cannot start with 0. Start with 1, then 0, then 2, 3, 5, 7, 9: 1,023,579. (0,123,579 is really 123,579, a 6-digit number.)

items.q: A freezer is at −18 °C. A fridge is at 4 °C. How many degrees warmer is the fridge?
items.e: Count in two jumps through 0. From −18 °C to 0 °C is 18. From 0 °C to 4 °C is 4. 18 + 4 = 22 degrees. Do not work out 18 − 4.

items.q: The population of a town, rounded to the nearest 10,000, is 250,000. What is the smallest the population could be?
items.e: Numbers from 245,000 to 254,999 round to 250,000. 244,999 would round down to 240,000, so the smallest is 245,000. (254,999 is the greatest.)

items.q: A charity raised £2,495,600. What is this to the nearest £100,000?
items.e: 2,495,600 is between 2,400,000 and 2,500,000. Look at the ten thousands digit: 9. 5 or more, so round up. Answer: £2,500,000.
